lessons.title: కుక్క, పిల్లి — the odd one out, and the word that most likely closes the loop
lessons.gloss: dog and cat — kukka genuinely breaks from its Dravidian cousins' shared naayi root, debated as onomatopoeic or a Sanskrit loan; pilli most likely closes the ENTIRE arc's cat-story loop, the probable Dravidian source behind Sanskrit's biDaala and so Hindi's billi

segments.text: Kannada just gave you a rock-solid native dog-word. Telugu breaks from that pattern — but its cat-word may be the single most important word in this whole arc.

blocks.title: The word, taken apart - కుక్క — genuinely the odd one out

segments.text: కుక్క (kukka, "dog") does not clearly continue the same నాయి-family root shared by Kannada, Malayalam, and Tamil. Its origin is honestly debated: some linguists propose it's onomatopoeic, imitating the sound of a bark; others propose a borrowing from Sanskrit कुक्कुर (kukkura, itself a similarly-shaped word for dog). Neither is settled — but either way, Telugu's everyday dog-word genuinely doesn't match its closest cousins.

blocks.title: The word, taken apart - పిల్లి — most likely closing the whole arc's loop

segments.text: పిల్లి (pilli, "cat") is a real, documented Proto-Dravidian root, pillV — with cognates surviving as rarer, alternate words for cat in both Tamil and Kannada. Here's why this word matters for the whole arc: Sanskrit's word for cat, बिडाल (biḍāla) — the word behind Hindi's बिल्ली (billī), which you met as "most likely" borrowed from Dravidian, without a confirmed specific source — most likely traces back to this exact root. So Telugu's everyday word for "cat" is most likely the closest living relative of the very word Sanskrit borrowed, tying together Latin's cattus/Arabic's qiṭṭ story on one side and Hindi's billī story on the other, all in one word.

segments.instruction: "kukka" — dog, genuinely different from its Dravidian cousins
segments.source: [YOU SAY: "kukka" — dog, genuinely different from its Dravidian cousins]

segments.instruction: "pilli" — cat, most likely the source behind Hindi's billī
segments.source: [YOU SAY: "pilli" — cat, most likely the source behind Hindi's billī]

segments.text: Does కుక్క continue the same root as Kannada's nāyi? (No — genuinely different, debated between onomatopoeia and a Sanskrit loan.) What is పిల్లి most likely the source of? (Sanskrit's बिडाल, biḍāla — and so Hindi's बिल्ली, billī.)

lessons.title: ఎ — one character, met inside words you already say
lessons.gloss: the single character ఎ — recognised inside words you already say

needs: a pen and something to write on
your eyes, for letter shapes on the page
notice.text: Before we start: this one needs your hands, so it is not a driving lesson. You will want a pen and something to write on and your eyes, for letter shapes on the page. You can listen to everything else now — leave the sections called Script you'll notice: ఎ and Guided Practice until you have stopped, and I will say so again when we reach it.

segments.text: Before the new one: డ — what does it do?
One character this time. Just one — and you have been saying it for pages without knowing which mark on the page it was.
It is an independent vowel — the shape the vowel e takes when a word begins with it, rather than the sign it becomes inside a word.
You already say these, and every one of them has ఎ somewhere inside it:
మీరు ఎలా ఉన్నారు? — how are you? (respectful).
ఆరు ఏడు ఎనిమిది తొమ్మిది పది — six to ten.
నలుపు తెలుపు ఎరుపు నీలం — black, white, red, blue.

blocks.title: Writing: ఎ — copy what you see

segments.text: Use two pen-down runs. Start at the central junction. Turn down and left around the compact lower loop, then continue around its base until you return to that junction. Lift once. Restart at the junction and sweep through the broad outer arch, climbing to the high left tip.

That is three numbered movements: 1–2 stay joined; 3 restarts after the lift. The order follows Sathish Shanmugam's Write Telugu Alphabets tracing guide and is fitted here to the printed Noto Sans Telugu shape. Telugu schools do vary in how they teach the hand, so learn this as one sourced order rather than the only possible way anyone writes ఎ.

segments.instruction: at these words, and find ఎ in the ones that have it
segments.source: [YOU LOOK: at these words, and find ఎ in the ones that have it]

segments.instruction: ఎ three times — lower loop, lift, broad outer arch — saying e as you finish each one
segments.source: [YOU TRACE: ఎ three times — lower loop, lift, broad outer arch — saying *e* as you finish each one]
